title: Can You Tell If Something Was Made by AI? The New Labeling Rules, Explained
summary: New EU rules require chatbots to identify themselves and deepfakes to be labeled. Here's what that actually means for spotting AI content - and where the gaps remain.
before: AI companies made voluntary promises about watermarking and labeling. No enforcement, no deadlines, inconsistent implementation.
after: EU AI Act mandates transparency: chatbots must disclose they're AI, deepfakes need labels, and AI-generated content must carry machine-readable marks.
body:
The EU AI Act's transparency rules took effect on August 2, 2026. For the first time, there are actual legal requirements - backed by fines up to 15 million euros - forcing AI companies to help you know when you're talking to a machine or looking at synthetic content. But the gap between what the rules require and what you can reliably verify on your own is wider than most coverage suggests.

## What the New Rules Actually Require

<cite index="8-3,8-4,8-5">Under the new rules, chatbots and other interactive AI systems must tell users they are dealing with AI, not a human. Deepfakes - images, videos, or audio that have been edited or generated using AI - must be labeled.</cite> <cite index="8-6">AI-generated or altered content must also carry machine-readable marks so it can be detected more easily.</cite>

<cite index="5-2,5-3">These obligations require providers and deployers of AI systems to be transparent about the use of AI in four key areas: direct interaction with individuals, AI-generated content, emotion recognition and biometric categorization, and deepfakes and AI-generated text on public-interest matters.</cite>

<cite index="2-1,2-2">The obligations apply immediately from August 2, 2026 to all in-scope systems, regardless of when they were placed on the market. Content generated and published before that date need not be retroactively labeled.</cite>

## How the Big AI Labs Are Responding

**Google** has the most mature system. <cite index="10-6,10-7">SynthID is an invisible watermark that Google DeepMind embeds into content produced by its AI systems. SynthID is one of the most ambitious provenance efforts shipping today.</cite> <cite index="10-8">By May 2026, Google reported that more than 10 billion pieces of content had been watermarked with it.</cite> <cite index="11-3">At Google I/O 2026, the company confirmed its invisible AI watermark is rolling into Google Search and Chrome, with OpenAI, Kakao, and ElevenLabs signing on as adopters.</cite>

**OpenAI** announced a dual-layer approach. <cite index="14-2">Images generated with ChatGPT, Codex, and its API now include C2PA metadata and a SynthID watermark - the two leading protocols for identifying AI images.</cite> <cite index="14-14">OpenAI put it this way: "Watermarking can be more durable through transformations such as screenshots, while metadata can provide more information than a watermark alone."</cite>

**Anthropic** (Claude's maker) went furthest on text. <cite index="32-8">Every Claude model launched on or after August 2, 2026 now embeds an invisible statistical watermark directly into generated text - and applies that mark globally, not only in Europe - making Claude the first major frontier AI lab to deploy production-scale text watermarking across all its products at once.</cite>

## What You'll Actually See on Platforms

<cite index="23-2,23-3">TikTok's AI generated content policy in 2026 requires visible labeling on all AI-generated visuals and audio that depict realistic people or scenes. The platform uses C2PA Content Credentials to detect synthetic media automatically, even when creators do not self-disclose.</cite> <cite index="26-3">TikTok has labeled over 1.3 billion AI-generated videos through automated detection.</cite>

<cite index="28-10">LinkedIn is the clearest outlier. In May 2026 it became the first major platform with a confirmed policy that demotes - rather than removes - content specifically because it reads as generic AI.</cite>

The browser-level integration is perhaps most useful. <cite index="12-13,12-14">As Google's CEO put it, users can "simply circle to search an image, or right click in Chrome and ask, 'Was this generated with AI?'" The browser checks the file for the SynthID signal and its content credentials and reports what it finds - no upload, no separate tool.</cite>

## The Honest Limits

Here's where it gets complicated. These systems work best when content flows through controlled channels without modification. In the real world, that's not how most content travels.

<cite index="10-14">Metadata gets stripped the moment you screenshot an image or paste text into a new document.</cite> <cite index="37-20">Screenshots, compression, cropping, aggressive editing - all of these can strip or degrade an embedded watermark.</cite>

For text watermarks specifically, <cite index="42-6,42-7">the statistical signal depends on the specific token distribution the model produced. Any rewriting that substantially changes which words and tokens appear - including asking a different AI model to rewrite the text - will defeat the watermark signal.</cite>

<cite index="9-11">SynthID's text detection is less reliable at 70-85% for lightly edited content, dropping to 40-60% for heavily paraphrased text.</cite>

And there's a deeper problem: <cite index="41-4,41-5,41-6,41-7">a detected mark is not proof of AI authorship. "Claude may not be the original author. People often use Claude to proofread, translate, summarize, or convert files. The output can carry a Claude mark even if the underlying ideas, text, or data originated from another source."</cite>

## What This Means for You

The new rules represent genuine progress. AI companies now have legal obligations and infrastructure to mark their outputs. Major platforms are building automated detection. You can check individual images in Chrome or upload files to verification portals.

But treat labels as evidence, not proof. A missing label doesn't mean something is human-made - the mark may have been stripped during editing or sharing. A present label doesn't mean AI wrote everything - it may just have polished someone's draft. <cite index="37-25">Watermarking isn't a guarantee - it's a best effort.</cite>

The systems work best for catching bulk synthetic content and obvious deepfakes. They're less reliable for the messy middle - content that's been edited, remixed, or passed through multiple hands. For high-stakes decisions about what's real, you'll still need judgment, not just technical verification.
